units.text: 12. The Book of the Future Must Also Know When to Be Quiet
A Stable Core and Help on Request

Let us design a book of the future without the obligation to fill it with every feature technology can offer. The first thing is the work: an identifiable text, with a structure and a version. Readers must be able to say what they are reading and return to the same passage. Corrections are welcome, but their traces must remain visible. An improved edition must not erase the memory of the criticism that made it necessary.

The second thing is freedom of access. The text can have adjustable type, audio playback, clear navigation, and compatibility with accessibility tools. These are not ornaments. They can determine who has the opportunity to encounter the work. A sophisticated interface that excludes readers for whom the simple format worked is not a universal improvement.

The third thing is help that does not seize the initiative. A glossary opens when you need it. An explanation shows you where it begins. An animation clarifies a relationship. An assistant preserves the distinction between text and interpretation. Readers can close every layer and continue with the work. This ability of the interface to withdraw seems to me a more important measure of quality than the number of features.

The fourth thing is continuity. Bookmarks, notes, and position within the work should be reasonably easy to preserve and move between forms. It is not useful for text and audio to be two disconnected worlds, or for notes to disappear along with a service. These are proposed requirements for durable cultural products, not assumptions about what every platform already offers.

The fifth thing is privacy. The questions we ask a book can reveal fears, beliefs, or personal circumstances. We should not assume that every interaction must be collected for good reading to exist. The American Library Association treats confidentiality in library use as a condition of intellectual freedom. This is an American institutional ethical reference point, not a description of every legal system. Yet the principle deserves serious consideration when designing digital reading. [ 24 ]

A printed book can be observed, its purchase can leave traces, and its notes can be read by someone else. It is not magically invisible. But the text on the table does not need to tell a service how long I lingered over a passage. We can ask a digital product for comparable discretion in features that do not require a connection. Technology should explain why it needs data, rather than treating readers’ curiosity as a resource available by default.

The sixth thing is preserving an ending. Not every conclusion needs to trigger a new recommendation immediately. Sometimes the work can be allowed to end. Readers need the option of disengaging without being instantly pulled toward the next object. A product that respects its ending acknowledges that its value can continue outside the interface.

All of these things can be done well or badly. A stable core can become rigidity; personalization can become fragmentation; explanation can become excessive supervision. No architecture automatically resolves every tension. But we can establish a priority: the tool must increase readers’ freedom and ability, not their dependence on an intermediary.

In this future, the publisher does not necessarily disappear. Its role can become more explicit: ensuring coherence, source quality, accessibility, and clear boundaries between layers. Authors remain responsible for what they sign. The automated system must be identified wherever it contributes. Readers must be able to distinguish the published work from an answer generated later, during conversation.

Such a book is no less a book because it can speak. It becomes less of a book if there is no longer anything stable to encounter, if every disagreement is smoothed away, and if the work changes solely to confirm your profile. Good adaptation also preserves resistance: the text’s right to say something other than what you would have ordered.
A Life with Reading, Without the Tribunal of Pages

We need not end with a universal quota of pages per day. A quota can help someone build a habit, but it is not the moral unit of a life. There are periods when we read a great deal and periods when we can barely open a book. Loving reading does not require us to despise the life that interrupts us. Sometimes someone needs us, and the book can wait.

A better beginning is to choose a purpose. Do I want to find my bearings in a field? I can start with an overview and a few definitions. Do I want to learn to do something? I need explanation, demonstration, and practice. Do I want to follow an argument? A book or a substantial essay may be suitable. Do I want an artistic experience? I do not have to justify it through productivity. Stating our purpose keeps us from asking one medium to provide every benefit.

Then comes choosing a level of difficulty we can live with. A book that is too easy may repeat what we know; one that is too difficult may require an introduction. There is no shame in changing the route. Readers need not prove anything to authors through suffering. Nor should they give up at the first resistance. It is worth asking whether the difficulty conceals an important idea or merely careless presentation.

We can create a simple space for reading: a text chosen before the available time begins, a convenient place, and fewer voluntary interruptions. This is a personal experiment, not a guaranteed treatment. We observe what helps us and adjust. One reader may prefer paper, another a device, another alternating with audio. The aim is the encounter with the work, not the victory of a material preference.

The right not to finish is useful too. A book may be unsuitable right now, poor, or simply less important than another. Giving up should not automatically be confused with superficiality. At the same time, it is worth distinguishing justified abandonment from a reflexive flight toward anything new. Only readers, with a certain honesty toward themselves, can make this distinction in a particular case.

Reading can become social without losing its inner time. A group can discuss a passage instead of organizing a parade of general opinions. Everyone can show where their interpretation begins. Disagreement thus becomes something we can check. We do not argue only about what the book seemed to be saying; we return to the shared object. Conversation does not replace reading; it gives it a second life.

Schools could cultivate this relationship through practices that make understanding visible without reducing the work to an official answer. A student can defend an interpretation and be asked which passage justifies it. They can compare an excerpt with an adaptation. They can use a digital assistant and check where it oversimplified. What matters is learning the difference between accessing an answer and constructing a justification.

The public library has a mission here that goes beyond storage. It can offer access, quiet, guidance, and gatherings around texts. For those who lack these conditions at home, they are not cultural accessories. They are an infrastructure that makes reading possible. Defending the book in public life therefore also means defending the places and people that make reading practicable.

We should also allow a way of reading that requires no explanation to anyone. No photograph, no score, no message about what we have finished. Not because sharing is bad, but because an experience’s value need not depend on publishing it. We can read something that interests us without turning it into an identity.

Ultimately, a life with reading is not a life from which films, podcasts, and conversations disappear. It is one in which each can find its place without colonizing all the others. Perhaps the reader of the future will not read in the same way as the idealized reader of the past. Yet they will have to preserve an old and difficult ability: not to confuse having received an answer with having finished thinking.
